question: Can wide-network training be analyzed as an interacting-particle system to prove global convergence and quantify finite-width and stochastic-gradient errors?

key_findings.claim: The paper exactly rewrites a width-n function approximator as an empirical distribution of interacting parameter particles whose energy is the mean-squared approximation loss.
key_findings.evidence: The model averages coefficients times parameterized kernels; one-body target terms and pairwise kernel terms form the particle energy, and the empirical weighted measure turns the represented function into a convolution.

key_findings.claim: In the infinite-width limit, gradient descent follows a nonlinear Liouville or Wasserstein gradient-flow equation and converges to the target function under the stated positivity and discriminatory-kernel assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3.1 gives a law of large numbers and commuting large-width/long-time limits. Convexity in distribution space eliminates non-global stationary solutions for the function approximation problem.

key_findings.claim: Finite-width gradient-descent fluctuations begin at central-limit scale but heal to order n to the minus one at sufficiently long times.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3.2 identifies an n-to-the-minus-one-half Gaussian fluctuation process that decays, while Proposition 3.3 states the late representation error is smaller than n to any power below minus one after times growing faster than log n.

key_findings.claim: Mini-batch SGD becomes a stochastic differential equation with multiplicative, state-dependent noise that vanishes as the approximation error vanishes.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 24 uses noise strength theta equal to step size divided by batch size; the induced stochastic PDE extends Dean's equation, and its quadratic variation depends on the prediction residual rather than a constant temperature.

key_findings.claim: Appropriate batch-size or step-size scaling preserves the deterministic infinite-width limit and controls the stochastic error order.
key_findings.evidence: With theta proportional to n to the minus 2-alpha, Proposition 4.1 recovers the same limiting flow. Propositions 4.2-4.3 show asymptotic representation and loss errors can be quenched, with alpha one requiring batch size on the order of n squared in the example prescription.

key_findings.claim: Numerical scaling supports the predicted n-to-the-minus-one discrepancy on a difficult target but does not test modern supervised networks or architecture effects.
key_findings.evidence: Single-layer ReLU and sigmoid networks approximate spherical three-spin functions in dimensions up to 50 over widths 10,000 to 60,000. The conclusion states the theory is insensitive to architecture and leaves kernel, depth, regularization, and optimal-design questions open.

method.core_idea: Lift finite neural parameters into an evolving probability measure, where mean-field particle dynamics make the function-approximation objective convex and finite-width corrections analyzable.
method.mechanism: Gradient flow moves each particle according to target and pairwise interaction potentials. As width grows, the empirical measure converges to a deterministic nonlinear PDE; central-limit expansion yields finite-width fluctuations. Mini-batch sampling adds multiplicative noise whose strength is controlled by step-to-batch ratio.
assumptions: Training examples can be freshly sampled from a large-data distribution rather than repeatedly drawn from a finite dataset.
The last layer is wide and scaled as an empirical average, with suitable positive initialization density.
Mean-squared function approximation and a discriminatory kernel accurately represent the learning problem.
Batch size or step size scales with width as required for the selected asymptotic regime.

techniques.role: Represents neuron parameters as an interacting particle population.
Describes deterministic infinite-width gradient dynamics in distribution space.
Separates leading mean-field behavior from Gaussian finite-width fluctuations.
Models mini-batch error as state-dependent stochastic forcing.
Couples width, time, batch size, and step size to derive asymptotic error rates.

evaluations.setting: Theoretical wide final-layer kernel and neural representations under gradient flow.
evaluations.metric: Almost-sure function convergence and asymptotic fluctuation order.
evaluations.result: The deterministic measure flow reaches the target and finite-width error improves from n^-1/2 transient scale toward n^-1 at long times.
evaluations.baseline: Existential universal approximation without an optimization guarantee.

evaluations.setting: Mini-batch SGD with width-dependent noise strength.
evaluations.metric: Law-of-large-numbers limit and asymptotic representation and loss error.
evaluations.result: The same leading flow is recovered, and stochastic error can be controlled by batch-size or step-size schedules.

evaluations.setting: ReLU and sigmoid one-hidden-layer networks approximating random spherical three-spin targets in dimensions 10, 25, and 50.
evaluations.metric: Empirical loss and signed discrepancy versus width.
evaluations.result: Ten target realizations show approximately linear n^-1 scaling in the displayed log-log plots.
evaluations.baseline: The theoretical asymptotic slope rather than another optimizer or model family.

limitations: The analysis assumes a large-data or online-sampling limit and omits repeated finite-dataset correlations.
The strongest results concern mean-squared function approximation and a wide averaged layer, not classification cross-entropy.
Required batch scaling can be impractical, including an n-squared example for the sharpest stochastic rate.
Numerical experiments use shallow networks and synthetic target functions.
Architecture, representation learning in earlier layers, normalization, dropout, and realistic data structure are intentionally unresolved.
failure_modes: Finite-width networks may remain outside the asymptotic convex distribution regime.
A degenerate kernel or insufficiently supported initialization can violate convergence assumptions.
Finite reused datasets introduce temporal noise correlation absent from the SDE derivation.
Fixed batch size and learning rate can leave stochastic fluctuations larger than the claimed n^-1 scale.
Deep bottlenecks or feature-learning interactions can make last-layer particle independence misleading.
reusable_insights: Analyze neurons as a population distribution when permutation symmetry makes individual identities irrelevant.
Track SGD noise as state dependent because gradient variance shrinks near an exact interpolant.
State the order of width, time, data, batch, and step-size limits explicitly.
Distinguish universal representability from convergence of a specified optimizer.
open_questions: Which finite-width and finite-time bounds make the asymptotic theory predictive for practical widths?
How does sample reuse change the multiplicative-noise PDE and error floor?
Can comparable convergence and fluctuation results cover deep feature learning and cross-entropy?
Which architectures and kernels optimize the constants hidden by asymptotic rates?

competitive_landscape.title: A Mean Field View of the Landscape of Two-Layer Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Concurrent mean-field analysis of two-layer neural-network optimization and landscape structure.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mei et al. establish distributional dynamics and convergence properties; this paper additionally emphasizes long-time n^-1 fluctuation scaling and multiplicative mini-batch noise.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Over-parameterized Models using Optimal Transport
competitive_landscape.relationship: Concurrent optimal-transport treatment of global convergence in measure-parameterized models.
competitive_landscape.difference: Chizat and Bach focus on global convergence of Wasserstein gradient flows; Rotskoff and Vanden-Eijnden derive finite-width central-limit and stochastic-gradient error scaling around the mean field.

competitive_landscape.title: Mean Field Analysis of Neural Networks: A Law of Large Numbers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Concurrent propagation-of-chaos and law-of-large-numbers analysis for wide networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sirignano and Spiliopoulos center deterministic mean-field convergence; this paper extends the agenda to asymptotic fluctuations, long-time healing, and mini-batch multiplicative noise.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Provably Optimizes Over-parameterized Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Alternative over-parameterization route to optimization guarantees.
competitive_landscape.difference: Du et al. give finite-network convergence through local kernel-like stability; the particle paper takes an infinite-width distribution limit and characterizes representation and SGD fluctuations.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a dynamical universal approximation theorem for SGD, convexity in the infinite-particle limit, and n^-1 long-time error with controllable stochastic fluctuations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: It is an important member of a concurrent 2018 mean-field cluster. The distinctive value is the fluctuation and long-time error analysis plus state-dependent SGD noise, while practical relevance is bounded by shallow function-approximation, online-data, and asymptotic assumptions.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete ten-page NeurIPS paper, including particle formulation, all propositions, SDE/SPDE derivation, three-spin experiments, and outlook. Four concurrent or competing primary arXiv theories were checked on 2026-08-23.
